questions.q: At 9 pm on 19 November 2026 in Delhi, which nakshatra is the Moon in, which tithi is it, and when does each change?
questions.do: Set Your place to Delhi and Night of to 19 November 2026. Move the Time slider to about 9:00 pm and read Tonight's nakshatra.
questions.a: The Moon is in Purva Bhadrapada (पूर्वभाद्रपदा), the 25th nakshatra, and it is Shukla Dashami, the 10th tithi. The Moon moves into Uttara Bhadrapada at about 6:57 am on 20 November, and Ekadashi starts at about 7:17 am. Each nakshatra is 13°20′ of sky, and the Moon covers that in about a day.

questions.q: On the night of 24 November 2026 in Delhi, how full is the Moon and when does it rise?
questions.do: Set Your place to Delhi and Night of to 24 November 2026. Read The Moon card and Sunset in The night.
questions.a: Full Moon, 100% lit. It rises around 4:55 pm, close to sunset (about 5:24 pm). A bright Moon washes out faint stars that night.

questions.q: On 21 December 2026, whose night is longer: Srinagar's or Thiruvananthapuram's?
questions.do: Set Night of to 21 December 2026. Pick Srinagar, then Thiruvananthapuram, and compare Sunset and Sunrise in The night.
questions.a: Srinagar: sunset about 5:25 pm, sunrise about 7:32 am, about 14 hours. Thiruvananthapuram: about 6:09 pm to 6:31 am, about 12.4 hours. In December, places further north have longer nights.

questions.q: On 21 June 2027, the page says London is never fully dark. Why? Compare with Delhi.
questions.do: Set Night of to 21 June 2027. Pick London, then Delhi, and read Fully dark in The night.
questions.a: London shows never fully dark. Delhi is fully dark from about 8:56 pm. London is far north (51.5°N), so in midsummer the Sun never sinks far enough below the horizon. Twilight lasts all night.

questions.q: This page uses work done by earlier astronomers. Which star catalogue gives the bright stars' positions, and whose formulas give the planets' brightness?
questions.do: Read the footer at the bottom of the page.
questions.a: Star positions come from the Hipparcos catalogue. Planet brightness uses the formulas of Mallama and Hilton (2018). Planet orbits come from JPL's approximate elements (Standish and Williams).
